title: Would you play a game you knew was built to study and train your reactions?
author: True-Objective-2125
selftext:
**Hypothetical:** a game where an AI watches how you react (timing, hesitation, where you look) and reshapes the gameplay(itself) to push exactly what you are missing. It never hides that it's doing it, and you'd get measurably better.

But you'd also know that every run is a test. Would you play it?

Does knowing make it better(rewarding), because the challenge is honest, or worse, because it stops feeling like play?

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body:
Although I like the idea, I don't think it would be something that would be "rewarding". Actually I think it's the opposite 

It would punish you for becoming better at reacting to things, and the enemy would hide in you blind spots. When you finally get good at something that skill is now useless

It is the kind of mechanic that would go into a fast paced horror game.

replies.author: True-Objective-2125
replies.body:
Ok, hear me out, the skill is still useful. Say it's a reaction game: things flash and you tap. You're slow on one side, the machine knows, so it pushes you right to your real limit there. Then it moves on to the next weak spot.  
Now imagine that game is the job application. You don't send a CV, you play. Either you reach the level or you don't. It's not testing what you know, it's testing and training a human skill at the same time. Would you apply that way?

comments.author: AlphabetSoupKitchen
comments.body:
Games that adjust to how you play aren't new, but obviously mentioning anything A.I. related in the same sentence will induce hysteria.

Alien Isolation achieved this with complex behavior trees that unlocked or locked sections based on what items you used, where you tended to like to hide and such.

replies.author: True-Objective-2125
replies.body: Ok fair, Alien Isolation is a good one. The alien learns where you hide, so you can't keep using the same locker. But it adapts to beat you. Mine would adapt to train you. Same tech, different goal. And yeah, the word AI does half the arguing for you lol, Call it: adaptive difficulty

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
I'd play it, and I think knowing makes it better, as long as it's framed as "the game learns you" rather than "you're being tested." Players already accept that in roguelikes and in dynamic difficulty, and the openness is what makes it feel fair instead of rigged.

The risk is the one Heath_co points out: if it always targets your weak spot, it never lets you enjoy what you're good at. I'd give the player some breathing room, maybe one run in three that plays to your strengths, so getting better actually feels like getting better and not just like the goalposts moving.

replies.author: True-Objective-2125
replies.body: The game learns you, same idea, different narrative. And one round in 3 to make you taste progress. Noted 🗒️

comments.author: Mrbuttshaman
comments.body: For sure.  If it was like an fps like unreal tournament 1999 and it actively trained you to get better, I'd find that amazing.  If it was like a puzzle game where it shifted it's targets based on your ability to solve puzzles, that would also be amazing.  Same with math or really anything like that.  I would expect some difficulty structure with caps(like resident evil 4 adjust itself based on player success) but overall I think it would be good.

comments.author: pianokayak
comments.body: What do you mean the game thinks?

replies.author: True-Objective-2125
replies.body: I would like to think of it as a high level of computing.

comments.author: StoneCypher
comments.body:
It's completely orthogonal to my decision making process.  I wouldn't care either way.

What motivates me is the kind of gameplay.  Do this on Starcraft?  I'm in, because I like starcraft.  Do this on Quake?  I'm out, because I'm bored of Quake.
